extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; scholars studying Schopenhauer and metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-by-chapter abstract and index of Schopenhauer's Essay on the Fourfold Root of the Principle of Sufficient Reason, summarising its taxonomy of forms of the principle and related conceptual distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Homogeneity and Law of Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato and Kant recommend obedience to two laws as the method of all knowledge: the law of Homogeneity (attend to resemblances to form species and genera) and the law of Specification (distinguish species and lower kinds carefully; do not prematurely subsume individuals under a genus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These transcendental laws presuppose nature is in harmony with them. Schopenhauer faults previous treatments (including Kant's) for neglecting the law of Specification and argues the principle of sufficient reason must be analysed with both laws in view.

rubrics_metrics.name: General formulation of the Principle of Sufficient Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Nihil est sine ratione cur potius sit, quam non sit — 'Nothing is without a reason why it should rather be than not be.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the general expression covering the different forms of the demand 'Why?' which underlies all science; the necessity it refers to is of different kinds across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold root: classification into four forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The relations that constitute the root of the principle fall into four classes (the 'fourfold root'), corresponding to four distinct forms in which the principle of sufficient reason appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer treats these four classes in chapters IV–VII and uses them as the exhaustive taxonomy for applications of the principle across perception, judgment, pure intuition (space/time), and inner volition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical form (ground of knowing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of the principle valid for judgments: a judgment must have a ground (another judgment) to express knowledge; when it has such a ground its predicate may be called true (formal or logical truth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer delineates four kinds of grounds for judgments (another judgment, sense-perception, conditions of experience yielding synthetic a priori, and the formal conditions of reason yielding metalogical truth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical form (law of causality / becoming)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the class of ideas of perception (objects of experience under space and time), the principle appears as the law of causality: when a new state appears it must have been preceded by another from which it regularly follows (cause → effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law pertains exclusively to changes of objects of external experience (fatal to cosmological proofs of God); Schopenhauer further distinguishes three modes of causation relevant to different domains: cause proper, stimulus, and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical form (law of being)
rubrics_metrics.description: With space and time as pure intuitions, parts determine one another so that the law according to which parts of space/time determine one another is the law of sufficient reason of being (basis of geometry and arithmetical truths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In space every position is determined with reference to every other; in time every moment is conditioned by preceding moments. Ground-of-knowledge here produces conviction distinguished from insight into ground-of-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral form (motives and volition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The class of objects that is the immediate object of inner sense — the subject in volition — yields the moral form: when a motive appears every human or brute will perform the only act that accords with its inborn and unalterable character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject knows itself not as knowing but as willing; motivation is causality viewed from within, leading Schopenhauer to argue that freedom of will is an absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three modes of causation: cause, stimulus, motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature exhibits three forms of causation: (1) cause in the narrow sense (where Newton's third law applies and effect proportional to cause), (2) stimulus (lacking proportionality), and (3) motive (requires knowledge and characterizes animal action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modes account for distinctions among inorganic bodies, plants, and animals; only 'cause proper' fits mechanical reciprocity; 'motive' presupposes intelligence and explains why freedom of the will is incoherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four kinds of grounds for a judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment may have as its ground: (1) another judgment (logical/formal truth), (2) sense-perception (material truth), (3) forms of understanding and sensibility giving synthetic a priori judgments, or (4) the formal conditions of reason giving metalogical truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer uses this to classify truths and to argue there is no 'intrinsic' truth divorced from relation to something outside the judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metalogical judgments / laws of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal conditions of reason yield four metalogical judgments (laws of thought): (1) a subject equals the sum of its predicates, (2) a subject cannot both have a predicate affirmed and denied, (3) of two contradictories one must belong to every subject, (4) truth is the relation of a judgment to something outside it as its sufficient reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are laws about form rather than material content; reason has only formal truth according to Schopenhauer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wolff's threefold division (historical taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wolff divided the doctrine of the principle into three kinds: principium fiendi (cause), principium essendi (possibility/being), and principium cognoscendi (ground of knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer credits Wolff with first completely distinguishing meanings of the principle; he situates earlier thinkers (Leibniz, Kant, Hume) in relation to this taxonomy and then refines it into his fourfold scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status and limits of proofs of the principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to prove the principle of sufficient reason are futile because any proof of the principle presupposes the principle itself (exhibiting the ground of a judgment presupposes the demand for a ground).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer argues the principle is the expression of the demand for grounds; seeking a further proof leads to circularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between understanding and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding apprehends causal relations directly (creates the objective world as phenomenon via the law of causality), whereas reason produces judgments that have grounds (truth as relation to grounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, arithmetic and abstract conceptual operations are not functions of the understanding; understanding's proper form is causal apprehension, not the Kantian system of twelve categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner sense and the impossibility of knowledge-of-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject cannot become an object of knowledge; the self knows itself only as willing (inner sense), not as knowing — 'there can be no knowledge of knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underlies Schopenhauer's treatment of volition as a distinct class of objects for the subject and supports the moral-form classification of the principle.
